Only slightly. There's a small fee, and she pays it without a second thought.
It's 2014, at an airport in China. Dawn Michelle Hunt, an American from Chicago, is checking two bags for the next flight of a trip she won.
Not long after, security staff call her aside. She is led into a room, and her two bags are already there.
The officers want to know one thing. Are these bags hers?

Why would she say anything else? She packed them herself. She just paid to carry them.
Inside the luggage are designer handbags. And sewn into the linings of those handbags, authorities say, is more than two kilograms of methamphetamine.
Her family says she had no idea it was there. She believed the handbags were a prize, from the people who had paid for the trip of her life.
The luggage was hers. The drugs, she said, were not.
Three years later, a court sentences her to death, with a two-year reprieve. Today, she is serving life.

voice.text: Before China, there was Chicago.
Dawn was a daughter and a sister. A former flight attendant. An artist who loved fashion, and loved to travel.

Her brother Tim remembers her as intelligent, and trusting. She and their mother liked to enter sweepstakes, he told Reuters. For Dawn, every entry was a small possibility that something wonderful might happen.

In 2014 she was working as a receptionist, in a family that had given decades to public service. Her father, Gene, had served in the Army and then as a Chicago police sergeant. Tim had been a Chicago police officer himself.
A family that knew what danger looked like.
What arrived in Dawn's inbox didn't look like danger at all.
It looked like she had won.

The message said she'd won a contest. Accounts differ on exactly what the prize was: cash, travel, or both. But every version has the same shape. An unexpected win, and people ready to fly her across the world.
Dawn didn't believe it. Not at first. Tim says she looked the organizers up online. What she found looked real enough that she sent her passport details.
Then the thing that ended her doubts arrived.
The tickets.
Real tickets to Hong Kong, paid for by someone else.
That is what makes this story so hard to shake. The first part of the promise was true.
Her family believes the deception was hidden in everything that came after.
According to Tim's sworn account, Dawn spent nine days in Hong Kong. Sightseeing. Shopping. The people running the trip treated her well, and every expense was covered.
Then they offered more: mainland China. With their help she got a visa, and spent about nine more days travelling through the country.
Watch what those days did.
The email became a ticket. The ticket became a city. And the city became a relationship, with people who had given her nothing but reasons to trust them.
There was more to come. Australia, she was told. Another part of the prize.
For Dawn, the trip of her life was still going.
But before she left China, they had one more gift for her.
Just before the next leg of the trip, the organizers told Dawn she had won something else. Designer handbags.
She accepted them. Why wouldn't she? These were the people who had paid for weeks of her life.
But there was a problem. Her luggage was already full.
So, Tim testified, she went with people from the trip to the Baiyun Leather Market, where the organizers bought an extra bag.
Dawn packed the handbags herself. Two pieces of luggage. Both checked in her name.
And at the check-in desk, the scale said what you already know.
Overweight.
She paid the fee.
Tim put that detail in his testimony for a reason. To him, it shows how ordinary this journey felt to his sister.
The people behind the trip had given her the handbags. They had solved her luggage problem. And whatever was hidden in those linings was now travelling in her name.

voice.text: At the airport, security staff call her aside. Tim says she is led into a room, and there are her two bags.

She has no reason to say anything else. They are her bags.
Then authorities find what is inside the linings.
Think about the two conversations happening in that room. Dawn believes she is identifying her luggage. The officers are investigating drug smuggling.
The same room. The same bags. The same word. Two different meanings.

One detail doesn't fit neatly. Dawn told her family she was flying on to Australia. But Tim has acknowledged that a journalist saw a court account naming a different flight, a domestic one, to Qingdao. We haven't seen records that settle it, and we won't pretend to.
What isn't in dispute is this: drugs were found in luggage she had checked. And in 2014, Dawn Hunt was arrested in China.
The trip ended in that room. The case was only beginning.
For Dawn, the airport wasn't the end of a bad trip. It was the first day of a detention that would last about three years before any verdict.

Her family says she tried to cooperate. Tim testified that she answered investigators' questions, and gave them the emails she had received from the organizers. The same emails that had started it all.
It wasn't enough.

Her family also alleges something worse. In testimony to Congress in 2024, Tim said Dawn had told their father she was sexually assaulted in the detention facility. That allegation has not been independently established in the sources available to us.
